body:
What is the nanoscale?

Every material around us is made of atoms and molecules. These particles combine to form substances such as metals, plastics, glass and minerals. A material usually has familiar physical and chemical properties: copper conducts electricity, gold has a characteristic metallic appearance, and iron is attracted by a magnet under ordinary conditions.

However, when a material is made extremely small, some of its properties may change. A substance that behaves in one way as a large piece can behave differently when it consists of extremely small particles or structures. Understanding these differences is the foundation of nanoscience and nanotechnology.

The nanoscale

The nanoscale is conventionally the size range from approximately 1 to 100 nanometres (nm). A nanometre is one-billionth of a metre.

1 nm = 10-9 m = 0.000000001 m.

The prefix nano means one-billionth. For comparison, 1 micrometre (µm) equals 1,000 nm, while 1 millimetre equals 1,000,000 nm. A human hair is approximately 80,000–100,000 nm wide. Thus, even the larger end of the conventional nanoscale is much smaller than the width of a human hair.

Nanoscience, nanotechnology and nanomaterials

Although closely related, these terms have different meanings.

  • Nanoscience: The scientific study of matter and phenomena at the nanoscale, including how materials behave when their dimensions become extremely small.
  • Nanotechnology: The understanding, manipulation and controlled use of matter at the nanoscale to obtain useful properties, materials or devices.
  • Nanomaterial: A material that has at least one external dimension or an internal structural feature in the nanoscale. Examples include nanoparticles, nanotubes and extremely thin films.
  • Nanoparticle: A particle whose 3 external dimensions are in the nanoscale, generally approximately 1–100 nm.

A nanoparticle is therefore one type of nanomaterial, but not every nanomaterial is a nanoparticle. A long nanotube may have a nanoscale diameter while its length is much greater than 100 nm. Similarly, a thin coating may have a nanoscale thickness while covering a large surface.

Why does a material behave differently when its size decreases?

The atoms in a piece of bulk gold and those in a gold nanoparticle are still gold atoms. Simply making the sample smaller does not change gold into another chemical element. Nevertheless, the arrangement of atoms, the proportion of atoms exposed at the surface and the way electrons behave can alter the material's observable properties.

Two fundamental explanations are especially important.

1. Surface-area effects

As a material is divided into increasingly small particles, its total exposed surface area generally becomes larger relative to the amount of material. A greater proportion of its atoms are situated at or near a surface, where they can interact with surrounding substances.

This can influence chemical reactions, adsorption, dissolution rates and catalytic activity.

2. Quantum-size effects

Electrons in sufficiently small structures may behave differently from electrons in the corresponding bulk material. In some nanomaterials, especially semiconductor nanocrystals, restricting electron motion changes which energy states are available. This can change optical and electrical properties.

These effects become important under different conditions. A large surface-area-to-volume ratio is not the same phenomenon as quantum confinement. A material can exhibit one effect without exhibiting a strong or useful form of the other.

Does every material change at exactly 100 nm?

No. The conventional 1–100 nm range provides a useful scientific classification, but 100 nm is not a universal boundary at which all properties suddenly change. Some unusual behaviours emerge at much smaller dimensions; others depend on the material, its shape or its surrounding environment.

A further distinction is that objects made from nanomaterials may be much larger than 100 nm. For example, a sunscreen containing nanoscale zinc oxide or titanium dioxide particles is a macroscopic product, although some of its ingredients have nanoscale dimensions. Such particles can protect against ultraviolet radiation while producing less visible whitening than some coarser-particle formulations.

Prelims focus

  • 1 nm equals 10-9 m.
  • The conventional nanoscale extends from approximately 1 to 100 nm.
  • 1 micrometre equals 1,000 nm.
  • Nanoparticles have 3 external dimensions in the nanoscale; other nanomaterials may have only 1 or 2.
  • The 2 major explanations for unusual nanoscale behaviour are surface-area effects and quantum-size effects.
  • Trap: 100 nm is an approximate classification boundary, not a size at which every material suddenly changes its properties.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 3, 'Atoms and Molecules', section 3.2, printed pp. 33–34, 2018–19 printing; National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, 'About Nanotechnology' and 'Just How Small Is Nano?', accessed 13 November 2026; National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, 'Nanomaterials', Introduction, accessed 13 November 2026.]

title: The Nanoscale: Understanding Size and Its Effect on Materials

body:
Understanding surface area and volume

The surface area of a solid is the total area of its exposed outer surfaces. Its volume is the amount of space occupied by the solid.

A solid object contains atoms in its interior and atoms at its surface. Interior atoms are surrounded by neighbouring atoms within the solid. Surface atoms have a different local environment because part of their surroundings is outside the material.

When a large piece of a material is divided into many smaller pieces, new surfaces are exposed. Consequently, the amount of surface available to interact with air, water or other substances increases.

For particles of the same shape and composition, decreasing particle size increases the surface-area-to-volume ratio. The same quantity of material can therefore present much more exposed surface when divided into sufficiently small, separate particles.

A simple comparison using cubes

Consider a solid cube whose sides are each 10 nm long. It occupies a volume of 1,000 nm3 and has a total exposed surface area of 600 nm2.

Now imagine dividing it into 8 identical smaller cubes, each having sides of 5 nm. Their combined volume remains 1,000 nm3. However, if the smaller cubes are separated so that all their faces are exposed, their combined surface area becomes 1,200 nm2.

ArrangementTotal volumeExposed surface area
1 cube with 10 nm sides1,000 nm3600 nm2
8 separate cubes with 5 nm sides1,000 nm31,200 nm2

The smaller cubes have twice the combined exposed surface area, although the quantity of material is unchanged. This simplified example illustrates why breaking a material into smaller particles can increase its opportunities to interact with its surroundings.

Why are surface atoms important?

Atoms within the interior of a solid interact mainly with neighbouring atoms of that solid. Atoms at the surface can also come into direct contact with external molecules.

As particle size decreases, the fraction of atoms located at or close to the surface generally increases. Surface-related effects can therefore influence a larger proportion of the material.

The effect is particularly important for processes occurring at a solid's surface, such as chemical reactions, attachment of molecules and interactions with surrounding liquids or gases.

How increased surface area affects material behaviour

1. Chemical reaction rates

A chemical reaction involving a solid and another substance often takes place where the substances come into contact. If more of the solid's surface is accessible, more reaction sites may be available at the same time.

For example, finely divided iron may react with oxygen more rapidly than a compact piece of iron under comparable conditions. This illustrates a surface-area effect. At very small dimensions, additional changes in surface energy and electronic structure may also affect reactivity.

However, a large surface area does not guarantee that every substance will react rapidly. The chemical composition, temperature, surrounding substances and condition of the particle surface remain important.

2. Catalytic activity

A catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed overall by that reaction. Many solid catalysts work by allowing reacting molecules to interact at their surfaces.

Making a suitable catalytic material into nanoscale particles can expose more active surface sites per unit mass. This can improve catalytic performance or reduce the quantity of an expensive catalyst required.

For example, nanoscale precious-metal catalysts are used in technologies such as automotive catalytic converters, which help convert harmful exhaust pollutants into less harmful substances.

Important distinction: A nanoparticle is not automatically a catalyst. Catalytic activity also depends on the material's chemical nature and the reaction involved.

3. Adsorption of substances

Adsorption occurs when atoms, ions or molecules become attached to the surface of another material. A large accessible surface area can provide more places for adsorption.

Nanostructured materials may therefore be useful in filters, sensors and certain pollution-control systems. Their effectiveness also depends on which substances their surfaces can attract or retain.

Adsorption must not be confused with absorption, in which a substance enters the bulk of another material. A sponge absorbing water illustrates absorption, whereas molecules attaching to the surface of a solid illustrate adsorption.

4. Dissolution and dispersion

Small solid particles can dissolve more quickly than large pieces of the same substance because more surface is available for contact with the solvent. Powdered sugar, for example, usually dissolves more quickly than a large sugar crystal under comparable conditions.

This everyday comparison helps explain the importance of surface area, even though ordinary powdered sugar is not necessarily a nanomaterial.

Dissolution rate and solubility are different properties. Dissolution rate describes how quickly a substance dissolves. Solubility describes how much of it can dissolve under specified conditions. A smaller particle does not necessarily make the substance substantially more soluble at equilibrium.

Why nanoparticles sometimes lose their surface advantage

Very small particles may attract one another and form larger clusters. This tendency is called agglomeration when particles associate into clusters, often through relatively weak interactions.

When particles cluster together, some surfaces may become less accessible to the surrounding environment. Consequently, the useful surface area may decrease.

The behaviour of nanomaterials therefore depends not only on their original particle size but also on how they are dispersed, whether they remain separate and what surrounds their surfaces.

A large surface-area-to-volume ratio explains many nanoscale effects, but it does not make every nanoparticle highly reactive, soluble, catalytic or dangerous. The material and its environment determine the actual outcome.

Prelims focus

  • Smaller particles of the same shape generally have a larger surface-area-to-volume ratio.
  • A larger proportion of atoms lie at or near the surface as particle size decreases.
  • Greater accessible surface area can increase opportunities for surface reactions.
  • Nanocatalysts may expose more active sites per unit mass.
  • Adsorption means attachment to a surface; absorption means entry into the bulk of a material.
  • Trap: Faster dissolution does not necessarily mean greater equilibrium solubility.

[Sources: National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, 'What Is So Special About Nano?', section 'Scale at which surface behavior plays a larger role', accessed 13 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 4, 'Sorting Materials into Groups', section 4.2, printed pp. 28–31, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 6, 'Physical and Chemical Changes', sections 6.1–6.2, printed pp. 58–61, 2018–19 printing; National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, 'Applications of Nanotechnology', sections on environmental applications and catalysis, accessed 13 November 2026.]
